THOUGHT: 
1) Epidemiology and presentation fit a primary bone malignancy of adolescence — a 13-year-old boy with progressive focal femoral pain that awakened him from sleep.  
2) Laboratory signs (markedly elevated ESR and leukocytosis) indicate an inflammatory/tumor-associated reaction but are non‑specific.  
3) Radiographic description — multiple lytic lesions in the diaphysis/mid‑femur with several layers of new periosteal bone formation (“onion‑skin” layered periosteal reaction) — is classically described for Ewing sarcoma. Osteosarcoma is more often metaphyseal with a sunburst pattern or Codman triangle and produces malignant osteoid on biopsy. Osteomyelitis can mimic imaging and labs but typically shows acute inflammatory cells rather than a small round blue cell tumor on biopsy.  
4) Biopsy showing sheets of small round blue cells is characteristic of Ewing sarcoma / primitive neuroectodermal tumor (PNET) family tumors; these tumors commonly harbor an EWSR1–FLI1 t(11;22) translocation.  
5) The preceding blunt trauma was likely incidental/precipitating attention to the area rather than the cause of the lesion.  
6) Taken together — age, site (diaphyseal mid‑femur), layered periosteal reaction, systemic inflammatory markers, and small round blue cell histology — strongly indicate Ewing sarcoma.

DIAGNOSIS: Ewing sarcoma (Ewing family tumor) of the left femur.
